keyPoints: ["Epithelial tissue: secretes mucus, hydrochloric acid and pepsin","Connective tissue: supports the mucosa and links it to the muscular layer","Nervous tissue (neurons): controls and coordinates stomach movements and secretions"]
modelAnswer: The stomach is an organ made up of several tissue types working together. The inside of the stomach is lined by epithelial cells, which secrete mucus, hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin. Around this epithelial layer are layers of connective tissue and smooth muscle, along with glands, blood vessels and neurons. Connective tissue supports the tissues of the mucosa and connects it to the muscular layer. The smooth muscle (part of the muscular layer) contracts to move food through the gut, and neurons (nervous tissue) control and coordinate these movements and secretions.

keyPoints: ["Each organ (two or more tissues together) performs only one specific task.","A full body function usually needs several such specific tasks working together.","An organ system groups organs with related functions so their combined, coordinated action achieves what no single organ could do alone."]
modelAnswer: A single organ, on its own, is made of two or more tissues organised to do just one specific task, for example the heart pumps blood, the lungs bring in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, and the stomach digests food. But no single organ can carry out an entire complex body function by itself. An organ system is a group of organs with related functions that work together to accomplish a larger task that no one organ could do alone, for example the digestive system needs the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, liver and intestines all cooperating to process food and absorb nutrients. So multiple organs are needed to build an organ system because each organ contributes a specific, specialised part of the overall function, and combining these specialised contributions is what lets the system carry out its complete, coordinated task.

keyPoints: ["Epidermis: protects the leaf and prevents water loss; lower epidermis has stomata (guard cells) for gas exchange.","Palisade mesophyll: chloroplast-rich, main site of photosynthesis.","Spongy mesophyll: loosely arranged with air spaces, allows gas diffusion.","Vascular tissue: xylem transports water (root to leaf); phloem transports food (leaf to rest of plant)."]
modelAnswer: In cross-section, a leaf shows three main tissue layers. Epidermal tissue: a single outer layer of cells covering the leaf (upper and lower epidermis), coated with a waxy cuticle; its function is to protect the internal tissues and prevent water loss. The lower epidermis also carries tiny pores called stomata, each guarded by two chloroplast-containing guard cells that control the pore's opening/closing, allowing exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide and evaporation of water vapour. Mesophyll tissue: lies between the two epidermal layers and is divided into palisade mesophyll (two to three layers of cylindrical, chloroplast-rich cells, the main site of photosynthesis) and spongy mesophyll (loosely arranged, irregularly shaped chloroplast-containing cells with large air spaces between them that allow gases to diffuse). Vascular tissue: consists of xylem, made of long dead cells that transport water from the root to the leaf, and phloem, which carries the food made in the leaf to the rest of the plant. (Sketch: draw a cross-section with upper epidermis on top, palisade mesophyll below it, spongy mesophyll beneath that, a vascular bundle (xylem and phloem) in the middle, and lower epidermis with stomata at the bottom.)

modelAnswer: Mesophyll lies between the two epidermal layers of a leaf and is of two types. Palisade mesophyll consists of two or three layers of cylindrical cells that contain many chloroplasts, making it the main site of photosynthesis. Spongy mesophyll consists of loosely arranged, irregularly shaped cells that also contain chloroplasts, with large intercellular spaces between them; these spaces facilitate the diffusion of gases (CO2 and O2) within the leaf.

modelAnswer: The internal structure of a typical leaf consists of three tissue types arranged in layers. Epidermis: the outermost single-cell layer on both the upper and lower leaf surfaces, covered by a waxy cuticle that protects the leaf and prevents water loss; the lower epidermis carries stomata, each flanked by two guard cells (which contain chloroplasts) that open and close the pore to control gas exchange and water vapour loss. Mesophyll: found between the two epidermal layers, it has two sub-types - palisade mesophyll, made of two to three layers of tightly packed, cylindrical, chloroplast-rich cells just under the upper epidermis (the main photosynthetic tissue), and spongy mesophyll, made of loosely arranged, irregularly shaped chloroplast-containing cells with large intercellular air spaces that let gases diffuse easily to and from the stomata. Vascular tissue: bundles of xylem (long, dead, hollow cells carrying water and minerals from the root up to the leaf) and phloem (living cells carrying the food produced during photosynthesis from the leaf to the rest of the plant) run through the leaf, usually forming the leaf veins. (Sketch: a cross-section showing upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll with air spaces, a vascular bundle of xylem and phloem, and lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells.)
